notes: Car-jacking conviction appeal; fresh co-accused evidence and weak identification led to unsafe conviction finding.

enrichment.short_title: Davies: car-jacking conviction quashed on fresh co-accused evidence
key_facts: Leslie Davies was convicted with John Jason Cleaver of robbery in a car-jacking at Tipton after taking a Ford Orion and seizing keys to a Subaru.
Davies was seen in the Orion shortly before and in the Subaru shortly after the robbery, but witness descriptions and identification evidence did not match his distinctive appearance.
Cleaver, after failing his own appeal, gave evidence de bene esse exonerating Davies and admitting he had lied at trial.
The prosecution case rested on circumstantial continuity of occupation rather than positive identification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction after the full court had granted leave on no-case and fresh-evidence grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Davies' robbery conviction was quashed as unsafe in light of Cleaver's admissible evidence and the inadequacy of the identification case.
enrichment.ratio: Where identification and description evidence is weak and a co-accused's fresh evidence is capable of belief and consistent with the prosecution gaps, the court may receive it under section 23 and quash a conviction if the combined picture leaves the court unsure of its safety.
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have stopped the robbery case at the close of the prosecution evidence
Whether Cleaver's post-conviction evidence should be admitted under section 23
Whether circumstantial before-and-after sightings sufficed without reliable identification

confidence.notes: Facts, evidential reasoning and final quashing order are clearly recorded.

notes: BUAV judicial review on marmoset research licences; mixed permission outcome on severity, death and guidance issues.

enrichment.short_title: BUAV v Home Secretary: judicial review of primate research licensing
key_facts: The BUAV challenged Home Office decisions on Cambridge University marmoset research conducted under three project licences.
An undercover investigation produced a critical report; the Chief Inspector reviewed the licences and the Minister accepted his conclusions.
The claimant argued severity limits were misallocated, post-operative care was inadequate, and stock-animal welfare should be weighed in licensing.
Further challenges concerned whether death is an adverse effect and whether a water-and-food restriction note was statutory guidance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to apply for judicial review of Home Secretary decisions and policy under the 1986 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused on grounds 1, 2, 4 and 6; permission granted on ground 3 (whether death is an adverse effect) and ground 5 (status of the water and food restriction guidance note).
enrichment.ratio: Historical, expert-heavy challenges to accepted Chief Inspector findings may be refused for delay and difficulty in showing irrational acceptance of a detailed report; pure statutory construction issues of continuing relevance may still warrant permission.
legal_issues: Whether moderate severity limits were lawfully assigned to Cambridge primate protocols
Whether staffing levels permitted lawful moderate severity classification
Whether death of itself is an adverse effect under section 5(4)
Whether the water and food restriction note was guidance or a code of practice under section 21

confidence.notes: Permission dispositions on each ground are explicit though many factual disputes remain untried.

notes: Case stated on s139 blade offence; blunt butter-knife blade held within statutory wording.

enrichment.short_title: Brooker v DPP: blunt butter-knife blade under section 139
key_facts: Brooker was convicted in the magistrates' court of having a bladed article in a public place.
The article was a 10 cm butter-knife blade with no handle, sharp edge or point.
The only issue was whether the object fell within section 139(2) as an article having a blade.
Brooker argued a blunt butter knife was outside the mischief Parliament intended to proscribe.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Bexley Magistrates' Court to the High Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the magistrates were correct that the butter-knife blade without handle was a bladed article under section 139(2).
enrichment.ratio: Section 139(2) uses the unqualified phrase 'any article which has a blade'; although sharp knives are the paradigm case, the statute is not limited to inherently dangerous sharp blades and invites no case-by-case sharpness inquiry.
legal_issues: Whether section 139(2) requires the blade to be sharp or pointed
Whether R v Davies on screwdrivers limits the section to inherently dangerous blades
Whether Hansard assists construction of section 139

confidence.notes: Short judgment with clear statutory reasoning and affirmative answer to the stated question.

notes: Landmark leaving-care judicial review; pathway plan and personal adviser failings found unlawful.

enrichment.short_title: J v Caerphilly: unlawful failures under leaving care legislation
key_facts: J, a looked-after child with complex needs, drug history and literacy difficulties, was released from Ashfield YOI in January 2005.
Caerphilly failed to complete a timely needs assessment and pathway plan, shared documents with J only after litigation, and let the personal adviser draft the plan himself.
The pathway plans were vague, lacked dates and specialist support, and did not meet Schedule requirements.
J remained uncooperative, but Munby J held that could not excuse statutory non-compliance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim for declarations and mandatory orders requiring lawful leaving-care assessment, pathway planning and personal adviser appointment.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; declarations and mandatory orders were made requiring a new personal adviser and compliant assessment and pathway plan by specified dates.
enrichment.ratio: A pathway plan must clearly identify the child's needs and what is to be done about them, by whom and by when; a personal adviser may participate in but must not prepare the statutory assessment and plan, and an uncooperative child is no excuse for failing to comply with leaving care duties.
legal_issues: Whether the personal adviser's dual role invalidated the leaving care process
Whether assessments and pathway plans complied with regulations 6-9 and the Schedule
Whether the local authority failed to secure suitable pre-release accommodation

notes: Syndicated loan transfer trial; Argo Fund held valid transferee and entitled to judgment for USD 29.5m.

enrichment.short_title: Argo Fund v Essar Steel: validity of secondary-market loan transfers
key_facts: Essar Steel defaulted on a USD 40 million syndicated loan arranged by Bayerische Landesbank after steel prices collapsed.
The Argo Fund bought discounted tranches totalling USD 29.5 million on the secondary debt market via Clause 27.2 transfer certificates.
Essar argued transfers were limited to banks or other financial institutions engaged in primary lending and that an implied exchange-control term voided transfers.
Argo was a Cayman mutual fund investing in distressed debt, regulated indirectly through its managers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of Argo's claim for debt and damages after Essar's default under the facility agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Argo succeeded; valid transfers were effected and judgment was entered for USD 29.5 million plus interest, with the implied exchange-control term rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 27.2 restricts novations to a bank or other financial institution capable of lending under the agreement, which includes regulated secondary-market debt purchasers such as Argo; an implied term requiring Indian exchange-control approval of each transferee is unnecessary and inconsistent with the express contractual scheme.
legal_issues: Whether Transferees were limited to banks or other financial institutions
What 'other financial institution' means in a 1997 syndicated loan agreement
Whether Argo qualified as a Transferee
Whether ineffective transfers operated as assignments and whether an implied exchange-control term applied
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society
Aktieselskabet Olivebank v Dansk Svolsyre Fabrik

notes: Three Attorney General rape sentence references; Phipps and Basra increased, B left undisturbed.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney General's References: unduly lenient rape sentences reviewed
key_facts: Three Attorney General references challenged sentences for rape and related offences in domestic, child-stranger and drug-facilitated cases.
Justin Phipps received seven years after three violent rapes of his former partner ES shortly before and after her pregnancy termination.
B, aged 16, received five years' detention for raping a 12-year-old stranger plus one year consecutive for burglaries.
Parvinder Basra received four years after covertly drugging a woman with GHB and raping her twice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General references under section 36 of the 1988 Act for review of sentences considered unduly lenient.
enrichment.outcome: Phipps' rape sentences were increased to nine years; Basra's rape sentence was increased to eight years; B's six-year total detention was held lenient but not unduly lenient and was not increased.
enrichment.ratio: A sentence is unduly lenient only if outside the range reasonably open to the judge, applying Milberry starting points and aggravating features; domestic rapes may be as serious as stranger rapes, and youth mitigates but does not preclude substantial detention for section 5 child rape.
legal_issues: The correct Milberry starting point for repeated domestic rapes
Whether a six-year total sentence for a 16-year-old's section 5 rape plus burglaries was unduly lenient
Whether Basra's four-year sentence adequately reflected GHB-facilitated repeated rape
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference No 4 of 1989 (1989) 11 Cr App R(S) 517
R v Milberry [2003] 1 Cr App R 396
Attorney General's Reference Nos 37-45 of 2003 [2003] EWCA Crim 2973

notes: Case stated on resisting police officer; acquittal on s5 Public Order Act held consistent with lawful arrest.

enrichment.short_title: Burrell v CPS: resisting arrest after section 5 warning
key_facts: Burrell attended Harrogate police station as an appropriate adult and became abusive in the custody suite.
Sergeant Downham warned him under section 5(4) and arrested him after further offensive conduct.
Burrell struggled during arrest and was convicted of resisting a constable in execution of duty.
A separate section 5 charge was dismissed because no likelihood of harassment, alarm or distress was proved beyond reasonable doubt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Harrogate Magistrates' Court on alleged inconsistency between acquittal on section 5 and conviction for resisting arrest.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the two verdicts were not inconsistent because arrest required reasonable suspicion whereas conviction required proof beyond reasonable doubt.
enrichment.ratio: The lawfulness of a section 5(4) arrest depends on whether the officer reasonably suspected offensive conduct likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress; failure to prove the section 5 offence beyond reasonable doubt at trial does not negate that objective reasonableness.
legal_issues: Whether acquittal on section 5 necessarily invalidated the arrest for resisting
The test for offensive conduct under section 5(4)
Whether the magistrates' two verdicts were logically inconsistent

confidence.notes: Short case stated with clear distinction between suspicion and proof standards.

notes: Fatal road collision appeal; Monk v Warbey counterclaim rejected as not protecting third-party loss.

enrichment.short_title: Bretton v Hancock: Monk v Warbey claim limited to third-party victims
key_facts: Helen Bretton was injured when her fiancé Mark Bryant-Powell's uninsured Rover collided with John Hancock's Peugeot van.
The judge apportioned liability 75% to Hancock and 25% to Bryant-Powell, finding Bretton was a user in breach of section 143 for lacking third-party cover for Bryant-Powell's driving.
Hancock counterclaimed under Monk v Warbey for Bretton's breach of statutory duty, seeking 25% of her damages because Bryant-Powell's estate was impecunious.
Bretton had insured the Rover in her name but only for her own driving.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against judgment entering liability for 75% of damages and allowing Hancock's Monk v Warbey counterclaim for 25%.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Hancock's Monk v Warbey counterclaim failed and judgment was entered for Bretton for damages to be assessed against Hancock alone.
enrichment.ratio: The Monk v Warbey duty under section 143 protects third-party victims of uninsured use, not joint tortfeasors seeking contribution for pure economic loss; a user does not owe the statutory duty to indemnify another tortfeasor's contribution claim.
legal_issues: Whether Bryant-Powell's speed contributed causatively to the collision
Whether Bretton had an ownership interest and was a user of the Rover
Whether Monk v Warbey extends to a tortfeasor's failure to recover contribution from an impecunious uninsured driver
linked_authorities: Campbell v McFarland and Omagh Urban District Council [1972] NILR 32

confidence.notes: Central Monk v Warbey extension issue and appellate disposal are clearly reasoned.

notes: Asylum permission appeal refused; credibility findings and late medical evidence not errors of law.

enrichment.short_title: Birgani v SSHD: permission refused on Iranian asylum appeal
key_facts: The Iranian appellant claimed asylum based on political activity, alleged torture after graffiti arrest, and persecution by his step-brother.
The adjudicator rejected his account as not credible in a detailed decision.
On appeal the IAT admitted but discounted late medical evidence of foot scarring said to support torture, finding inconsistencies with earlier accounts.
The appellant also argued political activity in the UK would alert Iranian authorities.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal against the IAT's refusal of permission to appeal from the adjudicator.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; no arguable error of law was shown in the credibility findings or treatment of the medical evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh evidence that could and should have been before the adjudicator is not ordinarily admissible on appeal; disagreements with factual credibility findings and late medical evidence do not establish legal error warranting permission.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred in treating the medical report as inadmissible or immaterial
Whether inconsistencies between interview and medical accounts were fatal
Whether UK political activity created a fresh risk on return

confidence.notes: Permission refusal reasoning is clear though underlying facts remain contested.

notes: Mongolian government guarantee appeal; instrument held a surety not demand bond; Holme v Brunskill applied.

enrichment.short_title: Marubeni v Mongolia: government guarantee not a demand bond
key_facts: Marubeni Hong Kong sold machinery to Buyan under a deferred payment contract for USD 18.8 million.
The Mongolian Ministry of Finance issued an MMOF Letter described as a guarantee pledging payment on simple demand if Buyan defaulted.
Buyan defaulted after rescheduling agreements in 1998 and 1999 without government consent.
Marubeni argued the letter was a demand bond creating primary liability; Mongolia argued it was a surety discharged by variation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Cresswell J's decision that the MMOF Letter was a secondary guarantee discharged under Holme v Brunskill by refinancing variations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the MMOF Letter was a guarantee imposing secondary liability and was discharged by material variations without the guarantor's consent.
enrichment.ratio: Outside the banking context, a document described as a guarantee and promising payment only if amounts under the underlying agreement are not paid when due creates secondary suretyship liability; banking demand-bond authorities do not apply to government pledges lacking performance-bond hallmarks.
legal_issues: Whether the MMOF Letter was a demand bond or demand guarantee
Whether the Minister of Finance had authority to undertake primary liability
Whether February 1998 and April 1999 reschedulings discharged the guarantee under Holme v Brunskill
linked_authorities: Esal Commodities Ltd v Oriental Credit [1985] 2 Lloyd's Rep 546
Gold Coast Ltd v Caja de Ahorros del Mediterraneo [2001] EWCA Civ 1806
